curriculum.lesson_evidence: Historians compare the past and present to find what has changed and what has stayed the same (continuity). Both can be shown by evidence such as photographs, maps and the memories of older people.

lesson.child_mission: Historians compare the past and present to find what has changed and what has stayed the same (continuity). Both can be shown by evidence such as photographs, maps and the memories of older people.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same HSIE idea to a new place or source, then compare two pieces of evidence for strength.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Sort into change or continuity: trams replaced by buses; the post office is on the same corner; people still meet at the park on Saturdays.

FEEDBACK
Trams replaced by buses is change. The post office on the same corner and people meeting at the park are continuity.

WATCH FOR
Saying that everything has changed, or that nothing has, ignores the evidence that both happen.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Choose a place in your community. Use two sources such as a photo and an older person. Complete a Then / Now / Change / Continuity table with five rows. Suggest one cause of one change.

Write a short reflection naming one source or idea you corrected and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Historians compare the past and present to find what has changed and what has stayed the same (continuity). Both can be shown by evidence such as photographs, maps and the memories of older people.
materials: Optional: local map, photo or interview notes
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.
lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Choose a place in your community. Use two sources such as a photo and an older person. Complete a Then / Now / Change / Continuity table with five rows. Suggest one cause of one change. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Original response on new material: Trams replaced by buses is change. The post office on the same corner and people meeting at the park are continuity. Reasoning: I used change by attending to continuity and explain why it matters rather than copying the worked model.

Parent: Written model 2: Common error: Saying that everything has changed, or that nothing has, ignores the evidence that both happen. Correction: Trams replaced by buses is change. The post office on the same corner and people meeting at the park are continuity. Why: the correction restores accurate use of change.

Parent: Likely misconception: Saying that everything has changed, or that nothing has, ignores the evidence that both happen. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one likely error with change, correct it, and explain why the correction helps a reader or audience.

teach_steps.explain:
Historians compare the past and present to find what has changed and what has stayed the same (continuity). Both can be shown by evidence such as photographs, maps and the memories of older people.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on sources, places and respectful community knowledge, rather than guessing from a single picture. Keep every claim linked to evidence.

Read the worked example and name the sources, map features or community examples that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your record with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your evidence? If a detail is uncertain, identify what source you would need next. One deliberate, evidence-based revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
